title: Ricefields to piggery: Questions over land conversion for 50,000-hog facility in Quezon
summary: Questions are raised over the conversion of irrigated ricefields in San Antonio, Quezon, into a 50,000-hog piggery, with residents seeking answers about tenant farmers’ rights and the government…

blocks.text: 1st of two parts
QUEZON PROVINCE, Philippines – How did a 12-hectare tract of land formerly planted to rice become the site of a massive piggery designed to accommodate as many as 50,000 hogs?
For more than two years, Emma Alday, now in her eighties, has been seeking answers from government agencies about the development of Mighty Livestock Farms in Barangay Callejon, San Antonio, Quezon.

For Alday, whose own farm lies just 250 meters from the development, the issue raises questions about the protection of irrigated agricultural land, the rights of tenant farmers, and the government approvals that allowed the project to proceed.

Despite numerous inquiries, visits to government offices, and an appeal to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. bearing approximately 300 signatures from concerned residents, Alday says she has yet to receive a satisfactory explanation.
According to Alday, the property was purchased approximately two years before construction began. At the time, residents had no idea that the land would eventually be used for a large-scale piggery.

“They bought it mga 2 years before construction, tinanggal nila ang tubigan. Walang kamalay-malay ang mga tao na piggery pala (They removed the irrigation system. The people had no idea it was going to be a piggery),” she recalled.
By the time residents learned what was being planned, the development was already moving forward.
What particularly troubles Alday is that the property was formerly irrigated riceland.

Under the Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act, irrigated lands and irrigable lands covered by existing or planned irrigation projects are subject to stringent protections against conversion. The Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law also establishes requirements and restrictions governing the conversion of agricultural lands.
Alday says she personally approached the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) in May 2025 to verify the property’s irrigation status.
“Pinapunta pa ako ng DAR sa NIA to find out if the ricefield is part of the plan ng irrigation, so I inquired and kasali sa irrigated canal,” she said.
(The DAR even referred me to the NIA to find out whether the ricefield was included in the irrigation plan. So I inquired, and it turned out to be part of the irrigated area.)

Alday questioned the compensation received by tenant farmers who previously cultivated the land. She alleged that personnel from the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), rather than protecting the farmers’ interests, encouraged them to surrender their rights.
“DAR was even convincing the tenants to give up their land sa kahit anong halaga (in exchange for any amount),” Alday claimed.
The circumstances surrounding the farmers’ departure from the property, including whether their rights were adequately protected, remain among the issues she wants clarified.

The town government of San Antonio, however, maintained that the property was reclassified through a duly enacted municipal ordinance and that Mighty Livestock Farms complied with the documentary requirements for its development.

In an interview, Sangguniang Bayan Secretary Carlo Katigbak explained that Municipal Ordinance No. 112, passed in 2022, authorized the reclassification of the property from agricultural to agro-industrial use.

“The local council has authorized the reclassification of that lot from agricultural to agro-industrial use which carries with it the authority to build a piggery or feedmills, kasama siya sa (it’s included as) authorized usage under Municipal Ordinance 112,” Katigbak said.
He cited Section 20 of the Local Government Code of 1991, which grants local governments authority to reclassify agricultural lands within prescribed limits.
“Sa amin po naging 3rd class na po kami so if I’m not mistaken may cap na 10% and according to our municipal planning hindi pa sumusobra sa pinapayagan ng batas,” he explained.
(Our town is now classified as a third-class municipality, so if I’m not mistaken, the cap is 10%. According to our municipal planning office, we have not exceeded the limit allowed by law.)
He added that Barangay Callejon had been designated as an area for agro-industrial development.

“All requirements have been complied with at both local and national levels. With the Sangguniang Bayan and Panlalawigan, and with the DENR. So, there is no controversy yet, no cause of action,” Katigbak added.
But whether the matter has indeed been settled remains disputed by the affected residents.

While Section 20 of the Local Government Code authorizes local governments to reclassify agricultural land under specified circumstances, such authority is subject to applicable national laws and limitations.
Municipal reclassification is also legally distinct from the authorization to convert agricultural land to another use.

A copy of Municipal Ordinance No. 112 obtained by Rappler identifies documentary requirements that include certification from NIA that the land is not irrigated or covered by an irrigation project with firm funding commitments. It also requires certification from DAR concerning the property’s coverage under the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program (CARP), including whether it is subject to a Voluntary Offer to Sell or has been issued a Notice of Coverage.
Katigbak said the presumption was that both documents had been submitted, explaining that the ordinance was approved even at the provincial level.
However, the contents of those certifications and whether they establish that the property was legally eligible for conversion require clarification from the concerned agencies.
A closer examination of Municipal Ordinance No. 112 reveals another issue concerning the stated purpose of the land reclassification.
Section 2, which defines the purpose of the ordinance, reads: “The subject land shall be used exclusively for FEED MILL, being initiated by Mighty Livestock Farm Inc.”

This differs from the project description in the Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) issued by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) on October 24, 2023.

The ECC identifies the development as a livestock farm project with a maximum stocking capacity not to exceed 50,000 heads of pigs at any given time. The certificate covers a total land area of 113,973 square meters, or approximately 12 hectares.
The distinction is significant because the ordinance also contains a provision governing failure to implement its declared purpose.

Section 4, or the Self-Repealing Clause, states: “Failure on the part of the project initiator to fully implement or accomplish the hereto avowed purpose shall serve to automatically repeal or invalidate the authority hereby granted and restore subject land to its original classification.”

The provision raises questions about whether the livestock farm now being developed is consistent with the specific purpose for which the land was reclassified. It also raises the question of whether additional authorizations or amendments were secured to reconcile the municipal ordinance with the project described in the ECC.

The existence of different project descriptions does not, by itself, establish that a law has been violated. However, the discrepancy calls for an explanation from the government agencies responsible for approving and regulating the development.
The dispute highlights a broader concern over the protection of agricultural land, particularly irrigated ricefields that are subject to national restrictions on conversion.

While the municipal government maintains that the necessary requirements were complied with, Alday continues to question how land formerly used for rice production was approved for a development of this scale.

At the center of the controversy are the property’s irrigation status, the rights of its former tenant farmers, the documentary basis for its reclassification, and the difference between the purpose stated in the municipal ordinance and the project authorized under the ECC.
Whether the approvals obtained were sufficient to permit the development as it is now being constructed remains a matter requiring clarification from the responsible agencies.

For Alday and the residents who have joined her appeal, the questions go beyond a single property in Barangay Callejon. They are concerned with how agricultural land is protected, how government approvals are scrutinized, and whether communities can obtain clear explanations when the use of land on which they depend is fundamentally changed. (to be concluded)
